title: Boundaries Part 1
lead: Now we switch to grammar, and this is the highest-yield place to start. Sentence boundary questions appear in every module, and their rules are fully reliable. Once you know them, these are some of the fastest points on the test.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. The whole topic rests on one distinction: an independent clause, which can stand alone as a complete sentence, versus a dependent clause or fragment, which cannot.

A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb that together express a finished thought. “The scientist published her findings.” Subject: scientist. Verb: published. It can stand alone.

A fragment is missing a piece, or has a word that stops it standing alone. “Because the results were surprising” has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it waiting for the rest. “Having analyzed the data” has no working verb.

The words that turn a complete thought into a fragment are the subordinators: because, although, while, since, when, if, after, before, unless, whereas. A word group that starts with one of these cannot stand alone.

Every boundary question tests this. Each punctuation mark has rules about what it may join. Once you can tell sentences from fragments, the punctuation follows mechanically.

parts.title: Part 2 · How to read a boundaries question
parts.html:
Every boundaries question has a blank and the same instruction: complete the text so that it follows the conventions of Standard English. These questions test three things: how clauses are linked (this class), how extra information is set off, and what each punctuation mark may do (both in Class 16). Work in three steps:

  1. Investigate the blank. Where is it: inside a sentence, or between two clauses? Then compare the choices. What changes from one to the next: the punctuation, a conjunction, both?
  2. Find the focus. From what changes, name the rule being tested. If the blank sits between two independent clauses and the choices mix commas and conjunctions, the question is about linking clauses, and you can ignore everything else.
  3. Eliminate the errors. Put each choice into the blank and read the sentence. Cross out every choice that breaks the rule you named. One choice will be left.

Signs of a linking-clauses question: the choices add or remove commas and FANBOYS words; the choices add or remove a period or question mark; or any choice contains a semicolon.

Tip. The SAT does not test style. Only one choice is grammatically correct, and the other three each contain an error. A period and a semicolon do the same job between two sentences, so if two choices differ only in period versus semicolon, both are wrong.

parts.title: Part 3 · The connector menu
parts.html:
There are four ways to join two complete sentences, and the SAT tests all four.

ConnectorExampleRule
PeriodThe experiment failed. The team revised the protocol.Works between any two complete sentences.
SemicolonThe experiment failed; the team revised the protocol.Both sides must be complete sentences.
Comma + FANBOYS
(for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)		The experiment failed, so the team revised the protocol.A comma alone does not join two sentences.
Semicolon + transition + commaThe experiment failed; however, the team revised the protocol.However, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, consequently are adverbs. They cannot join sentences alone.

“The experiment failed, however, the team revised the protocol” is a comma splice, one of the test's favourite traps.

The colon. A colon needs a complete sentence before it. What follows can be a list, an explanation, or another sentence: “The team changed one thing: the temperature of the sample.” If the words before the colon cannot stand alone (“The team changed: the temperature”), the colon is wrong.

End punctuation has two rules.

  • It must match what the sentence does. A statement ends with a period even when it reports a question. “The guide asked whether anyone had seen the map.” is a statement. “The guide asked whether had anyone seen the map?” is wrong twice: the word order and the question mark.
  • It needs an independent clause on each side. “When the museum reopened in 2021. It drew record crowds.” is wrong, because the first part cannot stand alone. Use a comma instead.

A semicolon takes no conjunction and no dependent clause.

SentenceVerdict
The river froze early; which surprised the fishermen.Wrong. What follows the semicolon cannot stand alone.
The river froze early; and this surprised the fishermen.Wrong. A semicolon does not take a FANBOYS word.
The river froze early; this surprised the fishermen.Correct.

Subordination: joining a dependent clause to a sentence. A subordinator such as although, because, since, while, when, after turns a full sentence into a dependent clause, which can then be attached with a comma. This is a fifth way to repair a comma splice: “The results were surprising, the team published anyway” becomes “Although the results were surprising, the team published anyway.”

Where the comma goes. When a dependent clause comes first, a comma follows it: “Although the results were surprising, the team published.” When it comes second, there is usually no comma: “The team published although the results were surprising.”

parts.title: Part 4 · The error catalog
parts.html:
Every boundary question contains one of these errors. Learn to name it.

  • Comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. “The results were surprising, the team published anyway.” Fix: period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS.
  • Run-on (fused sentence): two complete sentences with nothing between them. “The results were surprising the team published anyway.” Same three fixes.
  • Fragment treated as a sentence: a period or semicolon with a fragment on one side. “The results were surprising; because the equipment had malfunctioned.” Fix: remove the semicolon and attach the fragment to the sentence.
  • Missing comma after an introductory clause: “Because the storm arrived early the game was canceled” needs a comma after “early”.
  • The “however” splice: “, however,” joining two sentences. The fix is a semicolon or period before “however”.

parts.title: Part 5 · The method at the seam
parts.html:
The four choices differ only in punctuation. Follow this procedure:

  1. Find the seam. On each side of the punctuation, ask: complete sentence or fragment? Check for a subject and a working verb. A subordinator (because, although, while) means that side is a fragment.
  2. Decide what is needed. Sentence + sentence needs a legal sentence connector: period, semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, or semicolon + transition. Sentence + fragment needs at most a comma.
  3. Test the choices. Does the punctuation match what the two sides need? Wrong choices fail in nameable ways: comma splice, fused sentence, fragment left standing alone, transition word with only a comma.
Example. The orchestra rehearsed daily, moreover, the conductor added new pieces to the program. Left: “The orchestra rehearsed daily” → complete
Right: “the conductor added new pieces to the program” → complete
Needed: a sentence connector. Comma + “moreover” is not one.
Fix: “…rehearsed daily; moreover, the conductor…” or a period.

The wrong choices will be the comma splice, a fused version, or a version that turns one side into a fragment.

parts.title: Part 6 · Is it a sentence?
parts.html:
Every rule in this class depends on one quick judgment: can this group of words stand alone? Most errors come from four cases where the instinctive answer is wrong.

WordsSentence?Why
The glacier melts.YesA subject and a working verb
It melts.YesA pronoun is a full subject. A sentence does not have to make sense out of context.
Today, it melts faster. / However, it melts faster.YesAn opening adverb or transition changes nothing
Many of them melt in summer.Yes“Many” is the subject
Many of which melt in summerNo“Of which” and “of whom” make the clause dependent
Which melts in summerNoA statement that starts with which, who, whose, where cannot stand alone
The glacier melting in summerNoA word ending in -ing is not a working verb without a helper
The glacier, which melts in summerNoThe verb belongs to “which”; the glacier still has no verb of its own
And the glacier melts.No (for these questions)It starts with a FANBOYS word

The second row matters most. Students feel that “It melts” or “They disagreed” is incomplete because it does not say what “it” or “they” is. Grammatically it is a whole sentence, so it needs a period or a semicolon in front of it, never a comma alone.

Warning sign. A comma followed by it, he, she, they, this or by however, therefore, today, then is very often a comma splice. When a choice has that shape, test whether a complete sentence stands on each side.

parts.title: Part 7 · Read to the period, and use the equivalents
parts.html:
Read the whole sentence. Wherever the blank is, start at the beginning of the sentence and read all the way to the period. The trap in these questions is a phrase that seems to finish the first sentence but in fact has to begin the second. Three kinds of phrase do this: a prepositional phrase, an -ing phrase, and a clause beginning with because, although or when.

Example. The cartographer Marie Tharp spent years plotting sonar readings of the Atlantic sea ______ she noticed a deep valley running along the middle of the ocean ridge. A) floor during this work
B) floor, during this work,
C) floor. During this work,
D) floor during this work, Read only as far as “during this work” and A looks fine. Read to the period and there are two complete sentences: “Marie Tharp spent years plotting sonar readings of the Atlantic sea floor” and “she noticed a deep valley…”. A and D run them together, and B joins them with commas alone. Only C separates them, and it shows that “during this work” belongs to the second sentence.

Check the strongest marks first. If one choice offers a period or a colon, start there. When the test gives you the option of making two sentences, it is often because two sentences are what the text contains.

The equivalents. Between two complete sentences these three do the same job:

period = semicolon = comma + FANBOYS word

A question can have only one correct answer, so if two or three choices are equivalent, all of them are wrong.

…although the two rivers once flowed side by ______ now runs forty kilometres to the east. A) side, the smaller one
B) side. The smaller one
C) side; the smaller one
D) side, but the smaller one B, C and D are equivalent, so none can be right. A is the answer, and the reason is at the start of the sentence: “although” makes the first clause dependent, so a comma is all it needs.

One conjunction for two clauses. That last example shows a second rule. A sentence that opens with although, because, while or since must not add but, and or so in front of the main clause: “Although the trail was steep, but the hikers reached the summit.” The first conjunction is usually far from the blank, so look back for it.

Comma before “and”? Use the period test. Replace “, and” with a period. If both sides are complete sentences, the comma is right. If the second part has no subject of its own, there is no comma.

SentencePeriod testVerdict
The dam was finished in 1936, and it still supplies three states.“It still supplies three states.” is complete.Comma correct
The dam was finished in 1936, and still supplies three states.“Still supplies three states.” is not.Wrong: remove the comma

A colon never follows “such as” or “including”. The words before a colon must be a complete sentence, and “The museum displays instruments such as” is not one.
